questions.q: Why is a Jupyter notebook's diff unreadable by default, according to this lesson?
options: Jupyter notebooks can't be committed to Git
A .ipynb file is JSON containing code, metadata, and base64-encoded image outputs, not plain text
Git doesn't support the .ipynb file extension at all
It's a bug in Git that will eventually be fixed
questions.explain: A notebook is a structured JSON document, not plain source — its diffs get buried in metadata and embedded binary output.

questions.q: What does nbdime do differently from a plain diff on a notebook?
options: It parses the notebook's actual structure, showing a readable code diff and rendered before/after plot comparisons
It deletes all notebook outputs automatically
It prevents notebooks from being committed at all
It converts the notebook into a .py file permanently
questions.explain: nbdime understands the notebook's JSON structure, so it can separate the real code change from embedded output noise.

questions.q: How does nbdime integrate with your day-to-day Git workflow after setup?
options: It requires replacing git diff with an entirely different command every time
It requires manually converting every notebook before each diff
It only works inside a special nbdime-only terminal
It wires directly into git diff, so the same command shows readable output automatically
questions.explain: Running `nbdime config-git --enable --global` routes git diff through nbdime automatically — no new commands to remember.

questions.q: Which of these is a habit this lesson recommends to reduce notebook diff noise, even without extra tooling?
options: Renaming the file to .py without changing its contents
Always committing every cell's output regardless of relevance
Never running the notebook before committing it
Clearing outputs before committing exploratory work
questions.explain: Clearing saved outputs strips embedded images and execution counts, cutting diff noise significantly.

questions.q: What does this lesson suggest doing once notebook logic becomes a real, reusable pipeline step?
options: Leave it in the notebook permanently, since notebooks are meant for production code
Convert the entire notebook to a PDF
Move it out of the notebook into an ordinary .py source file
Duplicate it across multiple notebooks for redundancy
questions.explain: A notebook that's become a real pipeline step is a strong signal that logic belongs in ordinary source code instead.
